questions.explanation:
Vertex AI Feature Store has a clear hierarchy: Feature Groups reference BigQuery sources, Features name individual attributes, Feature Views select and sync subsets into an online store, and the Feature Online Store provides the low-latency serving layer.

**Why this matching works:** Each resource has a single, distinct role; understanding the flow from source to serve makes the mapping unambiguous.

questions.question:
A bank is deploying a binary classification model that predicts loan approval. The compliance team requires that the model be audited for demographic bias before it goes live. The data science team has computed predictions for a test set that includes a protected attribute indicating applicant gender. They need to check whether the model approves loans at the same rate for both male and female applicants, regardless of actual creditworthiness.

Which fairness metric directly measures this requirement?

choices.text: Equal opportunity, which checks whether the true positive rate is equal across groups.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: Demographic parity, which checks whether the positive prediction rate is equal across the two gender groups.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: Predictive parity, which checks whether the precision of positive predictions is equal across groups.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: Individual fairness, which checks whether similar individuals receive similar predictions.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

skills: 6.1.2: Aligning with responsible AI practices (e.g., monitoring for bias).
questions.tip: Think about which fairness metric measures whether a model's positive predictions are distributed proportionally across groups, independent of true outcomes.
questions.explanation:
Demographic parity (also called statistical parity) requires that the proportion of positive predictions be the same across protected groups, irrespective of ground-truth labels.

**Why it works:** The compliance requirement is specifically about approval rate equality across gender groups, not about accuracy for qualified applicants. Demographic parity directly measures whether P(approve | male) = P(approve | female).

**Why the others don't work:**
- Equal opportunity: Conditions on ground-truth positives (creditworthy applicants), so it measures whether qualified applicants of each gender are approved at the same rate -- a different question.
- Predictive parity: Measures precision equality, i.e., whether approved applicants in each group are equally likely to truly be creditworthy -- again a different question.
- Individual fairness: Requires a similarity metric between individuals and assesses per-instance consistency rather than group-level approval rates.

questions.question:
During a review of the company's AI strategy, the ML team is asked to select a foundation model from Model Garden for a customer-facing summarization service. The service will process 50,000 documents per day, each up to 10 pages long. Cost per token is a primary concern and the team wants to avoid fine-tuning.

Which TWO factors should the team evaluate first when comparing Gemini variants in Model Garden for this use case? (Select 2)

choices.text: Per-token pricing for input and output tokens across available Gemini variants.
choices.explanation: At 50,000 documents per day, even small differences in per-token cost compound significantly; this is the primary cost lever.

choices.text: Maximum context window size to confirm the model can process a full 10-page document in one API call.
choices.explanation: A context window too small for 10-page documents forces chunking, which increases complexity and may increase total token usage.

choices.text: Multimodal input support for images and audio within the selected Gemini variant.
choices.explanation: The source documents are text-only; multimodal capabilities provide no advantage for this workload.

choices.text: Availability of supervised fine-tuning support for each Gemini variant.
choices.explanation: The team explicitly ruled out fine-tuning, so this criterion is irrelevant to the selection decision.

choices.text: Number of model parameters to estimate quality relative to model size.
choices.explanation: Model Garden does not expose raw parameter counts as a selection criterion, and parameter count alone does not predict summarization quality or cost.

skills: 1.2.1: Evaluating and selecting the appropriate model for a given task from Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Model Garden.
questions.tip: High-volume batch workloads have different priorities than interactive workloads - focus on what drives cost and throughput at scale.
questions.explanation:
For a high-volume summarization workload, input token pricing and output token length are the two most direct cost drivers, and context window must be sufficient for 10-page documents.

**Why it works:** Evaluating per-token pricing between Gemini Flash and Gemini Pro directly impacts the cost of 50,000 daily documents. Confirming the context window can fit 10 pages (roughly 8,000-15,000 tokens) ensures the model can process each document in a single call without chunking.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Model parameter count: parameter count is not directly exposed in Model Garden selection and does not reliably predict cost or summarization quality.
- Availability of supervised fine-tuning: the team explicitly wants to avoid fine-tuning, making this criterion irrelevant.
- Multimodal input support: the documents are text-based; multimodal capability adds no value here.

questions.question:
The operations team at a manufacturing company wants to detect product defects from assembly line images. They have 8,000 labelled images stored in Cloud Storage, split across four defect categories and one 'no defect' class. The team has no ML engineering experience and wants to avoid writing custom training code.

Which Agent Platform AutoML model type should they select?

choices.text: AutoML Video Classification, configured to sample one frame per video clip and classify the resulting still image.
choices.explanation: AutoML Video Classification is designed for temporal video sequences, not individual still images. Using it here adds unnecessary complexity without benefit.

choices.text: AutoML Image Classification (multi-class), trained on the labelled image dataset to assign one of the five categories to each new image.
choices.explanation: AutoML Image Classification is designed for categorising images into discrete classes. Multi-class is correct when each image belongs to exactly one category from a fixed set.

choices.text: AutoML Text Classification, trained on OCR-extracted text labels embedded in the images by the QA system.
choices.explanation: AutoML Text Classification operates on text content, not image pixels. It cannot analyse the visual defect patterns present in raw images.

choices.text: AutoML Tabular Classification, trained on metadata extracted from the images such as pixel statistics and colour histograms.
choices.explanation: AutoML Tabular Classification operates on structured feature data, not raw images. Using extracted statistics loses the spatial context needed for reliable defect detection.

skills: 1.1.4: Training models using Agent Platform AutoML.
questions.tip: Match the input data modality and output structure to the corresponding AutoML model type.
questions.explanation:
Agent Platform AutoML Image Classification is purpose-built for labelled image datasets where each image belongs to a single class. With 8,000 images across five classes, this falls comfortably within AutoML's supported data range.

**Why it works:** AutoML Image Classification trains a custom model on raw images using transfer learning, requiring no custom code, GPU setup, or ML expertise.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Tabular Classification: requires structured feature tables, not raw images.
- Video Classification: designed for temporal image sequences, not still images.
- Text Classification: operates on text content, not visual pixel data.

questions.question:
An e-commerce platform wants to build a product recommendation system. User interaction logs contain 200 million events across 50 million users and 2 million products. The team requires low-latency online recommendations and needs the model to capture complex, non-linear user-item interactions. Training budget is generous, but inference must complete in under 50 ms.

Which model type BEST satisfies the latency and interaction-complexity requirements?

choices.text: LLM with retrieval-augmented generation
choices.explanation: LLM inference latency is typically hundreds of milliseconds to seconds per query, which exceeds the 50 ms budget without aggressive caching and approximations.

choices.text: ARIMA
choices.explanation: ARIMA is a univariate time-series model and cannot model user-item interactions or produce ranked recommendation lists.

choices.text: DNN-based two-tower retrieval model
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: Logistic regression with hand-crafted features
choices.explanation: Logistic regression cannot capture the non-linear, high-dimensional interaction patterns at 50 M users x 2 M items scale without impractical feature engineering.

skills: 3.1.1: Choosing the model type (e.g., ARIMA, DNN, and LLM).
questions.tip: Consider which architecture can learn high-dimensional embedding spaces from implicit feedback at scale while still producing fast inference through approximate nearest-neighbor lookup.
questions.explanation:
A DNN-based two-tower model learns separate embedding towers for users and items, enabling sub-millisecond approximate nearest-neighbor retrieval at serving time, making it the standard architecture for large-scale recommendation.

**Why it works:** The two-tower architecture decouples user and item representations, so item embeddings are pre-computed offline and served via an ANN index. Query latency is dominated only by the user tower forward pass plus ANN lookup, easily fitting within 50 ms.

**Why the others don't work:**
- ARIMA: Designed for univariate sequential time-series, not multi-entity collaborative filtering.
- LLM with RAG: Generative inference latency far exceeds the 50 ms requirement at the scale described.
- Logistic regression: Cannot learn non-linear feature interactions at this dimensionality without extensive, brittle manual feature engineering.

questions.question:
The team is building a TFX pipeline and wants to detect schema anomalies in each new batch of training data before the training step runs. A team member adds the following components.

```python
from tfx.components import (
    CsvExampleGen, StatisticsGen, SchemaGen, ExampleValidator
)

example_gen = CsvExampleGen(input_base=data_root)
statistics_gen = StatisticsGen(examples=example_gen.outputs['examples'])
schema_gen = SchemaGen(statistics=statistics_gen.outputs['statistics'])
validator = ExampleValidator(
    statistics=statistics_gen.outputs['statistics'],
    schema=schema_gen.outputs['schema']
)
```

On the second pipeline run, the validator raises no anomalies even though a new feature was added to the data that was absent from the original schema. What is MOST likely causing this?

choices.text: ExampleValidator only detects anomalies in the training split and silently ignores the evaluation split, so new features that appear only in training are never flagged.
choices.explanation: ExampleValidator can validate both splits. The issue is that SchemaGen generates a fresh schema from the current data, not that evaluation splits are excluded.

choices.text: The CsvExampleGen component caches its output from the first run and does not re-read the updated CSV files, so ExampleValidator still sees the original feature set.
choices.explanation: TFX component caching can reuse previous outputs, but ExampleValidator's anomaly detection would not be silenced by CsvExampleGen caching if a fresh schema was also generated. The root cause is SchemaGen regenerating the schema from current statistics.

choices.text: ExampleValidator requires a minimum of three pipeline runs to establish a statistical baseline before it begins flagging schema deviations from the original schema.
choices.explanation: ExampleValidator compares current statistics against a provided schema immediately on each run. There is no minimum run count before anomaly detection activates.

choices.text: SchemaGen regenerates a new schema from the current run's statistics on every execution, so the new feature is included in the schema before ExampleValidator checks against it, suppressing the anomaly.
choices.explanation: SchemaGen derives a schema from the current batch's statistics. If SchemaGen runs on each pipeline execution, the generated schema always reflects the current data — meaning ExampleValidator finds no mismatch because the schema already includes the new feature.

skills: 5.1.1: Validating data and models within pipelines.
questions.tip: Consider what schema ExampleValidator is validating against — is it fixed from the first run or regenerated each time?
questions.explanation:
The pipeline regenerates the schema via SchemaGen on every run, so by the time ExampleValidator runs, the schema already includes the new feature. To detect deviations from an approved baseline, the schema should be curated and frozen (e.g., stored in a schema file and loaded via ImportSchemaGen) rather than regenerated from the current data. ExampleValidator then validates incoming statistics against the stable, human-approved schema.

**Why it works:** A fixed baseline schema captures the approved feature set. Any new or missing feature in incoming data produces an anomaly.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Split filtering: ExampleValidator validates all splits; split behaviour is not the cause.
- CsvExampleGen caching: even with cached data, a regenerated schema would match it.
- Three-run baseline: ExampleValidator has no such warm-up requirement.

questions.question:
An ML team is rolling out a new version of a high-stakes credit scoring model. Their rollout policy requires that the new model receives 5% of traffic for 48 hours, then 25% for another 48 hours, and only reaches 100% after the preceding stages show no degradation in precision and latency. If a stage fails, the previous model must be fully restored within minutes.

Which sequence of Vertex AI endpoint operations implements this CANARY deployment strategy?

choices.text: Deploy the new model to a separate endpoint and run shadow traffic by duplicating all production requests to it without affecting the primary model's responses.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: Deploy the new model version to the endpoint alongside the existing model; update the traffic split to 5/95, then 25/75, then 100/0 after each stage passes; if a stage fails, set the split back to 0/100 for the new model.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: Delete the existing model deployment and replace it with the new model, then roll back by re-deploying the old model from the registry if issues arise.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: Create a new endpoint for each stage, progressively shifting all traffic from the old endpoint to the new one by updating DNS records.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

skills: 4.1.4: Implementing model rollout strategies (e.g., A/B testing and canary deployments) to compare model versions.
questions.tip: A canary deployment gradually increases traffic to a new version in stages, with a rollback path if metrics degrade.
questions.explanation:
Incrementally adjusting the traffic split on a single endpoint while keeping both models deployed is the canonical canary deployment pattern on Vertex AI.

**Why it works:** Both models remain deployed throughout the rollout, so reverting to 0/100 instantly restores full traffic to the existing model without any redeployment delay. Each staged split is a lightweight API call that takes effect in seconds.

**Why the others don't work:**
- New endpoint per stage with DNS: DNS TTLs introduce propagation delays that prevent the minutes-level rollback required; also does not leverage the native traffic split feature.
- Shadow traffic to a separate endpoint: Shadow mode validates the new model's outputs but does not expose it to real production traffic, so business metrics cannot be measured.
- Delete and redeploy: Removing the existing deployment means rollback requires a full redeployment cycle, which can take several minutes and violates the quick-restore requirement.

questions.question:
An ML team is deploying a new version of their production fraud detection model that serves 10,000 online requests per second. They need to minimize customer impact from any regression in the new model's performance. The team wants to validate real production traffic patterns before committing to a full rollout, and they must be able to instantly revert to the current model if metrics degrade.

Which deployment strategy BEST satisfies these requirements?

choices.text: Batch prediction job
choices.explanation: Batch jobs process offline data and cannot serve real-time fraud detection requests at 10,000 requests per second.

choices.text: Blue-green deployment with immediate full traffic cutover
choices.explanation: Blue-green deployment switches 100% of traffic to the new version at once, which does not minimize customer impact during validation and makes rollback a deliberate re-switch rather than a traffic-percentage adjustment.

choices.text: Shadow deployment
choices.explanation: Shadow deployment sends copies of traffic to the new model but serves responses only from the existing model; it validates predictions in isolation but does not expose the new model to real consequence, so customer impact from a bad model is not observable.

choices.text: Canary deployment with traffic splitting on a Vertex AI endpoint
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

skills: 3.1.3: Choosing the deployment strategy.
questions.tip: Think about which strategy allows the new model to receive a small, controlled percentage of live production traffic while preserving an instant fallback path.
questions.explanation:
Canary deployment routes a small percentage of live production traffic (e.g., 5%) to the new model version while the existing model continues to serve the rest, allowing real-world validation with limited blast radius and instant rollback by adjusting the traffic split.

**Why it works:** Vertex AI endpoint traffic splitting lets the team set an exact percentage for the canary version. If latency or accuracy metrics degrade, the split is adjusted back to 0% for the new version within seconds.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Blue-green with immediate cutover: Exposes all 10,000 RPS to the new model at once, creating maximum customer impact if the model regresses.
- Shadow deployment: The new model's outputs are not served to customers, so any regression has no business impact, but neither does it validate end-to-end production behavior.
- Batch prediction: Cannot fulfill real-time fraud detection needs.

questions.question:
The operations team at a logistics company needs to forecast daily parcel volumes at 150 regional depots for the next 30 days. Four years of daily volume data is stored in BigQuery by depot and date. The team wants to minimise infrastructure overhead and keep predictions queryable via SQL.

Which BigQuery ML model type is MOST suitable for this workload?

choices.text: KMEANS to cluster depots by volume patterns and assign future volumes based on cluster centroids.
choices.explanation: k-means is an unsupervised clustering algorithm and does not produce time-series forecasts. It cannot predict future values.

choices.text: ARIMA_PLUS with the time_series_id_col option set to the depot identifier, producing per-depot forecasts in a single training job.
choices.explanation: ARIMA_PLUS supports multi-series forecasting via time_series_id_col, auto-tunes seasonality and trend, and outputs forecasts queryable with ML.FORECAST.

choices.text: BOOSTED_TREE_REGRESSOR trained on manually engineered lag features for each depot to predict the next 30 daily values.
choices.explanation: Boosted trees can model regression but require manual lag feature engineering and do not natively produce multi-horizon forecasts, adding significant complexity.

choices.text: LINEAR_REG with one-hot encoded depot IDs and date components such as day-of-week and month.
choices.explanation: Linear regression cannot capture autocorrelation or complex seasonality without extensive manual feature engineering, producing lower-quality forecasts than ARIMA_PLUS for time-series data.

skills: 1.1.1: Building models in BigQuery ML or Agent Platform AutoML (e.g., classification, regression, forecasting, and clustering) based on the business problem.
questions.tip: Think about which BigQuery ML model type is purpose-built for multi-series time-based prediction.
questions.explanation:
ARIMA_PLUS is BigQuery ML's native time-series model. The time_series_id_col option allows a single model to produce separate forecasts for each depot without training one model per series.

**Why it works:** ARIMA_PLUS automatically handles trend, seasonality, and holiday effects. ML.FORECAST returns predicted values per series queryable via standard SQL.

**Why the others don't work:**
- BOOSTED_TREE_REGRESSOR: can regress on tabular features but requires manual lag engineering and outputs only single-step predictions.
- LINEAR_REG: lacks autocorrelation modelling; underfits seasonal patterns without heavy feature engineering.
- KMEANS: unsupervised clustering — it does not forecast numeric outcomes.

questions.question:
A retail company is building a real-time product recommendation model. Feature values such as user click history and cart contents are computed daily in BigQuery and must be retrieved within 10 ms during online inference. The team wants to use Vertex AI Feature Store to manage this workflow.

Which Feature Store component must the team configure to satisfy the low-latency online serving requirement?

choices.text: A Feature Group pointing directly at the BigQuery table, queried at inference time using the batch serving endpoint.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: An offline Feature Store that materializes features to Cloud Storage Parquet files for direct model consumption.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: A Feature Online Store backed by Cloud Bigtable, with a Feature View that syncs from the BigQuery source on a defined schedule.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: A Vertex AI Dataset linked to the BigQuery table, used as the serving source through a deployed model endpoint.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

skills: 4.2.1: Managing and serving features using Agent Platform Feature Store.
questions.tip: Think about which Feature Store component is responsible for low-latency online reads at inference time.
questions.explanation:
The Feature Online Store (backed by Bigtable) is the component that provides single-digit millisecond feature retrieval for online inference.

**Why it works:** A Feature Online Store provisions a low-latency key-value backend (Bigtable or optimized embedding store). A Feature View syncs from the BigQuery Feature Group on a schedule, materializing the latest values so that online reads never touch BigQuery directly.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Batch serving endpoint: Designed for bulk offline reads; latency is orders of magnitude too high for real-time inference.
- Cloud Storage Parquet: An offline pattern; models cannot query Parquet files at sub-10 ms latency during serving.
- Vertex AI Dataset: Datasets are a training-time concept, not a serving-time feature retrieval mechanism.

questions.question:
A bank is building a credit approval model that must comply with fair lending regulations. Regulators require that for every declined application the bank can provide a ranked list of the specific input features that most influenced the decision. The data science team is evaluating which modeling technique to use.

Which approach BEST satisfies the regulatory interpretability requirement?

choices.text: k-means clustering
choices.explanation: k-means is an unsupervised clustering algorithm that assigns group membership; it does not produce the per-sample feature attribution required for declined-application explanations.

choices.text: ARIMA time-series model
choices.explanation: ARIMA is a univariate forecasting model and cannot classify credit applications or produce per-feature attribution for individual loan decisions.

choices.text: Deep Neural Network without any post-hoc explanation method
choices.explanation: A DNN without an explanation method produces only a prediction score; it cannot generate a ranked list of feature contributions for individual decisions.

choices.text: Vertex Explainable AI using Shapley values
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

skills: 3.1.4: Applying modeling techniques given interpretability requirements.
questions.tip: Think about which technique produces a per-prediction attribution score for every input feature, without requiring the model itself to be inherently simple.
questions.explanation:
Vertex Explainable AI uses Shapley values to compute a contribution score for each feature on every individual prediction, allowing the bank to tell each declined applicant exactly which features drove the decision.

**Why it works:** Shapley values have a solid game-theoretic foundation that satisfies the regulatory need for consistency and completeness. Vertex Explainable AI integrates directly with Vertex AI endpoints, applying SHAP or sampled Shapley attribution alongside each prediction.

**Why the others don't work:**
- DNN without explanation: Produces a probability score only; regulators require feature-level reasons.
- ARIMA: A time-series forecasting model with no ability to classify or attribute features for a credit decision.
- k-means: An unsupervised method that clusters data points; it does not generate per-decision feature attributions.

questions.question:
A data science team has trained a churn prediction model on Vertex AI. Each night, a marketing pipeline produces a CSV file in Cloud Storage containing 2 million customer records. The predictions are consumed by a batch reporting job the following morning and do not need to be served in real time.

Which serving approach is MOST appropriate?

choices.text: Deploy the model to a Vertex AI online prediction endpoint and have the reporting job call the endpoint once per record.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: Host the model on GKE with a Deployment of 10 replicas and send all 2 million records concurrently at startup.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: Submit a Vertex AI batch prediction job pointing at the CSV input in Cloud Storage and writing results back to Cloud Storage.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: Deploy the model to Cloud Run and schedule a Cloud Scheduler job to POST each record individually.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

skills: 4.1.1: Deploying models for batch and online inference using appropriate services (e.g., Agent Platform, Model Garden, Cloud Run, and GKE).
questions.tip: Focus on whether the use case demands low latency per-request responses or high-throughput processing of a fixed dataset.
questions.explanation:
Batch prediction jobs are purpose-built for processing large, fixed datasets asynchronously without requiring a persistent endpoint.

**Why it works:** Vertex AI batch prediction reads input directly from Cloud Storage or BigQuery, runs inference in parallel across managed infrastructure, and writes results back without the latency or cost overhead of a live endpoint.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Online endpoint per-record: Incurs endpoint provisioning costs and network round-trip latency for every record; designed for low-latency single requests, not millions of offline calls.
- Cloud Run per-record: Similar anti-pattern; using an HTTP service to fan out 2 million individual calls is inefficient and costly.
- GKE concurrent burst: Sending all records simultaneously without a managed queue would overwhelm the replicas and requires custom orchestration that Vertex AI batch prediction provides natively.

questions.question:
A retail company has deployed a customer-facing chatbot powered by Gemini. The security team is concerned that users could craft inputs that cause the model to reveal system prompt contents or exfiltrate data from the retrieval context. The company needs a managed solution that inspects both the user's input and the model's response without modifying the application's core inference code.

Which Google Cloud service BEST addresses this requirement?

choices.text: Add a Cloud Armor security policy to the load balancer in front of the Gemini API endpoint to block malicious HTTP payloads.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: Enable VPC Service Controls around the Vertex AI project to prevent data from leaving the perimeter.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: Configure Model Armor templates to evaluate prompts and responses for prompt injection, sensitive data, and policy violations before they reach the model and before they are returned to the user.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: Write a Cloud Function that computes a SHA-256 hash of each user message and rejects requests whose hash matches a blocklist.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

skills: 6.1.1: Building secure AI systems by protecting against unintentional exploitation and leaks of data or models (e.g., data exfiltration, malicious prompting, and sharing sensitive data with LLMs) using the appropriate security tool (e.g., Regex, safety filters, and Model Armor).
questions.tip: Think about which Google Cloud product is specifically designed to inspect LLM inputs and outputs for threats like prompt injection and sensitive data leakage.
questions.explanation:
Model Armor is Google Cloud's managed layer for detecting and blocking prompt injection, jailbreaking, sensitive data exposure, and policy violations in LLM traffic.

**Why it works:** Model Armor templates sit between the caller and the model, evaluating both the request and the response. This satisfies the requirement for inspecting inputs and outputs without requiring changes to inference logic.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Cloud Armor: Operates at the HTTP/network layer and inspects HTTP signatures, not LLM prompt semantics or model output content.
- VPC Service Controls: Restricts which Google Cloud services can be called from within a perimeter; it does not analyze the content of prompts or responses.
- Hash-based Cloud Function: Can only block exact or near-exact duplicates of known-bad messages; it cannot detect novel prompt injection attempts or data leakage patterns.

questions.question:
A retail company wants to adapt Gemini to generate product descriptions that consistently follow the company's brand tone, use specific formatting rules, and include custom metadata fields not present in the base model's default outputs.

Which tuning approach available in Vertex AI is BEST suited for adapting Gemini to this structured, style-specific output task?

choices.text: Model distillation using a larger Gemini Ultra model as teacher to compress its capabilities into a smaller model.
choices.explanation: Distillation reduces model size by transferring knowledge from a large model to a small one; it does not teach new domain-specific output patterns.

choices.text: Prompt engineering with a detailed system prompt that specifies tone guidelines and metadata fields, with no model weight updates.
choices.explanation: Prompt engineering alone is fragile - tone and structure can drift across diverse product inputs, and the base model may not reliably include all custom metadata fields.

choices.text: Reinforcement learning from human feedback tuning to train the model to prefer brand-compliant outputs based on human ratings.
choices.explanation: RLHF aligns general conversational quality preferences and is not designed to enforce deterministic output schemas or structured metadata fields.

choices.text: Supervised fine-tuning on Vertex AI using a dataset of (prompt, expected product description) pairs that demonstrate the required brand tone and metadata format.
choices.explanation: Supervised fine-tuning directly teaches the model to reproduce the desired output structure and tone from labeled examples, producing consistent results.

skills: 1.2.3: Building solutions and tuning models for specific use cases (e.g., Gemini, Imagen, Veo, and models as a service in Model Garden).
questions.tip: Think about which tuning method teaches a model to follow output patterns from labeled examples rather than updating its core knowledge.
questions.explanation:
Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on Vertex AI trains Gemini on labeled input-output pairs that demonstrate the desired brand tone, format, and metadata fields, making the model reliably reproduce the required output style.

**Why it works:** SFT adjusts the model weights using a dataset of (prompt, expected output) pairs, directly teaching the pattern of brand-compliant product descriptions with all required fields.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Prompt engineering alone: without fine-tuning, the model may drift from brand tone across varied inputs and long sessions; it cannot reliably enforce structural metadata fields.
- Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) tuning: RLHF is optimized for aligning conversational preferences, not for enforcing deterministic output schemas.
- Model distillation: distillation compresses a larger model into a smaller one; it does not teach new output styles or domain-specific formats.

questions.question:
A team runs a product recommendation model that is retrained on a fixed weekly schedule. Business stakeholders report that recommendation quality degrades noticeably within a few days after major promotional events, which cause sudden changes in user behavior. The team wants to adapt their retraining policy to respond to these changes more quickly without unnecessarily increasing retraining costs.

Which retraining policy should the team adopt?

choices.text: Increase the schedule frequency from weekly to daily retraining regardless of observed data distribution changes
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: Switch to continuous retraining by streaming all new user interactions directly into the training dataset and updating model weights in real time
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: Retain the weekly schedule but add a manual override process for data scientists to trigger retraining after promotional events
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: Trigger-based retraining: initiate a retraining run when Vertex AI Model Monitoring detects that data drift in key features exceeds a configured threshold
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

skills: 5.2.1: Determining an appropriate retraining policy.
questions.tip: Consider which policy directly responds to changes in the data distribution while avoiding unnecessary retraining when the data is stable.
questions.explanation:
Trigger-based retraining on data drift detection is the most appropriate policy for this use case.

**Why it works:** Vertex AI Model Monitoring continuously tracks feature distributions in production traffic and can emit an alert or trigger a pipeline run when drift exceeds a threshold. This ensures retraining happens promptly after promotional events that shift user behavior, while avoiding unnecessary retraining costs during stable periods.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Daily schedule regardless of drift: Retraining daily increases compute costs even during stable periods when model quality is not degraded, and may still miss intra-day shifts immediately after an event.
- Weekly schedule with manual override: Manual overrides depend on data scientists noticing the degradation and acting quickly. This is slow, error-prone, and does not scale as the number of models grows.
- Real-time streaming retraining: Continuously updating weights from a stream is complex to implement reliably, prone to catastrophic forgetting, and difficult to validate and roll back, making it a poor choice for a standard recommendation model.

questions.question:
A researcher is prototyping a neural network in Agent Platform Workbench and writes the following PyTorch training loop.

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(128, 64),
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(64, 1)
)
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
loss_fn = nn.BCELoss()

for epoch in range(10):
    for X_batch, y_batch in train_loader:
        pred = model(X_batch)
        loss = loss_fn(pred, y_batch)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
```

The loss does not decrease across epochs and the model converges to predicting the same value for every input. What is the MOST likely cause?

choices.text: The final nn.Linear layer outputs a single logit but BCELoss expects a probability, so the loss is always NaN, which PyTorch silently treats as zero and skips updates.
choices.explanation: BCELoss does expect values in [0, 1], so a missing sigmoid would cause NaN loss. However, NaN loss does not produce a converged-to-constant output — the model would exhibit erratic behaviour. The missing zero_grad is the MOST likely cause of the described symptom.

choices.text: nn.ReLU should be replaced with nn.Sigmoid in the hidden layer to prevent the dying ReLU problem, which causes all activations to become zero after the first epoch.
choices.explanation: The dying ReLU problem can reduce representational capacity, but it does not typically cause immediate convergence to a constant output in one or two epochs. Missing zero_grad is the more direct cause of gradient corruption.

choices.text: The learning rate of 1e-3 is too high for Adam on binary classification tasks and causes the loss to oscillate without converging, producing constant predictions.
choices.explanation: 1e-3 is a standard and widely used learning rate for Adam. While learning rate issues can impede convergence, the missing optimizer.zero_grad() is a code defect that directly corrupts gradient updates.

choices.text: optimizer.zero_grad() is never called, so gradients accumulate across batches and the parameter updates are corrupted by stale gradient values from previous steps.
choices.explanation: In PyTorch, gradients accumulate by default. Without calling optimizer.zero_grad() before loss.backward(), each backward pass adds to the existing gradients rather than replacing them, causing unstable or no effective learning.

questions.domain: Collaborating Within and Across Teams to Manage Data and Models
skills: 2.2.2: Developing models in Agent Platform Workbench or Colab Enterprise notebooks using common frameworks (e.g., PyTorch, sklearn, and JAX).
questions.tip: Look for a standard PyTorch training step that is missing between the end of one batch and the start of the next.
questions.explanation:
PyTorch accumulates gradients by default across `.backward()` calls. Without `optimizer.zero_grad()` at the start of each batch, gradients from batch N are added to those from batch N-1, N-2, and so on. This produces increasingly large and incoherent parameter updates, preventing the model from learning and causing it to collapse to a constant prediction.

**Why it works:** Adding `optimizer.zero_grad()` before `loss.backward()` resets all parameter gradients to zero, ensuring each batch produces a clean, independent gradient signal.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Missing sigmoid: causes NaN loss, not constant prediction convergence.
- Dying ReLU: reduces capacity gradually; does not instantly freeze outputs.
- Learning rate 1e-3: standard for Adam; not the cause of the described symptom.

questions.question:
The team is building a TFX pipeline and wants to detect schema anomalies in each new batch of training data before the training step runs. A team member adds the following components.

```python
from tfx.components import (
    CsvExampleGen, StatisticsGen, SchemaGen, ExampleValidator
)

example_gen = CsvExampleGen(input_base=data_root)
statistics_gen = StatisticsGen(examples=example_gen.outputs['examples'])
schema_gen = SchemaGen(statistics=statistics_gen.outputs['statistics'])
validator = ExampleValidator(
    statistics=statistics_gen.outputs['statistics'],
    schema=schema_gen.outputs['schema']
)
```

On the second pipeline run, the validator raises no anomalies even though a new feature was added to the data that was absent from the original schema. What is MOST likely causing this?

choices.text: ExampleValidator only detects anomalies in the training split and silently ignores the evaluation split, so new features that appear only in training are never flagged.
choices.explanation: ExampleValidator can validate both splits. The issue is that SchemaGen generates a fresh schema from the current data, not that evaluation splits are excluded.

choices.text: The CsvExampleGen component caches its output from the first run and does not re-read the updated CSV files, so ExampleValidator still sees the original feature set.
choices.explanation: TFX component caching can reuse previous outputs, but ExampleValidator's anomaly detection would not be silenced by CsvExampleGen caching if a fresh schema was also generated. The root cause is SchemaGen regenerating the schema from current statistics.

choices.text: SchemaGen regenerates a new schema from the current run's statistics on every execution, so the new feature is included in the schema before ExampleValidator checks against it, suppressing the anomaly.
choices.explanation: SchemaGen derives a schema from the current batch's statistics. If SchemaGen runs on each pipeline execution, the generated schema always reflects the current data — meaning ExampleValidator finds no mismatch because the schema already includes the new feature.

choices.text: ExampleValidator requires a minimum of three pipeline runs to establish a statistical baseline before it begins flagging schema deviations from the original schema.
choices.explanation: ExampleValidator compares current statistics against a provided schema immediately on each run. There is no minimum run count before anomaly detection activates.

skills: 5.1.1: Validating data and models within pipelines.
questions.tip: Consider what schema ExampleValidator is validating against — is it fixed from the first run or regenerated each time?
questions.explanation:
The pipeline regenerates the schema via SchemaGen on every run, so by the time ExampleValidator runs, the schema already includes the new feature. To detect deviations from an approved baseline, the schema should be curated and frozen (e.g., stored in a schema file and loaded via ImportSchemaGen) rather than regenerated from the current data. ExampleValidator then validates incoming statistics against the stable, human-approved schema.

**Why it works:** A fixed baseline schema captures the approved feature set. Any new or missing feature in incoming data produces an anomaly.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Split filtering: ExampleValidator validates all splits; split behaviour is not the cause.
- CsvExampleGen caching: even with cached data, a regenerated schema would match it.
- Three-run baseline: ExampleValidator has no such warm-up requirement.

questions.question:
The operations team at a manufacturing company wants to detect product defects from assembly line images. They have 8,000 labelled images stored in Cloud Storage, split across four defect categories and one 'no defect' class. The team has no ML engineering experience and wants to avoid writing custom training code.

Which Agent Platform AutoML model type should they select?

choices.text: AutoML Tabular Classification, trained on metadata extracted from the images such as pixel statistics and colour histograms.
choices.explanation: AutoML Tabular Classification operates on structured feature data, not raw images. Using extracted statistics loses the spatial context needed for reliable defect detection.

choices.text: AutoML Video Classification, configured to sample one frame per video clip and classify the resulting still image.
choices.explanation: AutoML Video Classification is designed for temporal video sequences, not individual still images. Using it here adds unnecessary complexity without benefit.

choices.text: AutoML Image Classification (multi-class), trained on the labelled image dataset to assign one of the five categories to each new image.
choices.explanation: AutoML Image Classification is designed for categorising images into discrete classes. Multi-class is correct when each image belongs to exactly one category from a fixed set.

choices.text: AutoML Text Classification, trained on OCR-extracted text labels embedded in the images by the QA system.
choices.explanation: AutoML Text Classification operates on text content, not image pixels. It cannot analyse the visual defect patterns present in raw images.

skills: 1.1.4: Training models using Agent Platform AutoML.
questions.tip: Match the input data modality and output structure to the corresponding AutoML model type.
questions.explanation:
Agent Platform AutoML Image Classification is purpose-built for labelled image datasets where each image belongs to a single class. With 8,000 images across five classes, this falls comfortably within AutoML's supported data range.

**Why it works:** AutoML Image Classification trains a custom model on raw images using transfer learning, requiring no custom code, GPU setup, or ML expertise.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Tabular Classification: requires structured feature tables, not raw images.
- Video Classification: designed for temporal image sequences, not still images.
- Text Classification: operates on text content, not visual pixel data.

questions.question:
A bank is deploying a binary classification model that predicts loan approval. The compliance team requires that the model be audited for demographic bias before it goes live. The data science team has computed predictions for a test set that includes a protected attribute indicating applicant gender. They need to check whether the model approves loans at the same rate for both male and female applicants, regardless of actual creditworthiness.

Which fairness metric directly measures this requirement?

choices.text: Predictive parity, which checks whether the precision of positive predictions is equal across groups.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: Demographic parity, which checks whether the positive prediction rate is equal across the two gender groups.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: Individual fairness, which checks whether similar individuals receive similar predictions.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: Equal opportunity, which checks whether the true positive rate is equal across groups.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

skills: 6.1.2: Aligning with responsible AI practices (e.g., monitoring for bias).
questions.tip: Think about which fairness metric measures whether a model's positive predictions are distributed proportionally across groups, independent of true outcomes.
questions.explanation:
Demographic parity (also called statistical parity) requires that the proportion of positive predictions be the same across protected groups, irrespective of ground-truth labels.

**Why it works:** The compliance requirement is specifically about approval rate equality across gender groups, not about accuracy for qualified applicants. Demographic parity directly measures whether P(approve | male) = P(approve | female).

**Why the others don't work:**
- Equal opportunity: Conditions on ground-truth positives (creditworthy applicants), so it measures whether qualified applicants of each gender are approved at the same rate -- a different question.
- Predictive parity: Measures precision equality, i.e., whether approved applicants in each group are equally likely to truly be creditworthy -- again a different question.
- Individual fairness: Requires a similarity metric between individuals and assesses per-instance consistency rather than group-level approval rates.

questions.question:
An MLOps team is setting up Vertex AI Model Monitoring for a newly deployed tabular regression model. The team lead reviews the configuration checklist and asks the team to identify the two components that are required to enable both skew detection and operational alerting. Without these two components, monitoring will either fail to start or fail to surface actionable signals.

Which two components are required? (Choose 2)

choices.text: A Cloud Composer DAG that exports prediction logs from BigQuery to Cloud Storage before the monitoring job runs.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: A Vertex AI Pipeline that re-trains and re-deploys the model automatically whenever a skew alert fires.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: An alerting notification channel (such as a Cloud Monitoring email or Pub/Sub notification channel) configured on the Model Monitoring job so that threshold violations are communicated to the team.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: A baseline dataset reference pointing to the training data (BigQuery table or Cloud Storage URI) so that the monitoring job can compute the reference distribution for skew detection.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: A custom Docker container image that packages the monitoring logic, uploaded to Artifact Registry before the monitoring job is created.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

skills: 6.2.1: Configuring and using Model Monitoring on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform to establish continuous evaluation metrics for production models.
questions.tip: Think about what Vertex AI Model Monitoring needs to compare live traffic against, and how the results surface to the operations team.
questions.explanation:
Skew detection requires a baseline to compare against, and operational alerting requires a notification channel. Both are necessary for the monitoring setup to fulfil its purpose.

**Why it works:** The baseline dataset gives the monitoring job the reference distribution against which it measures divergence. The notification channel is how the job communicates that a threshold has been exceeded; without it, alerts are computed but never delivered.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Retraining pipeline: Automated retraining is a response action that can be added later; it is not required for monitoring to start or alert.
- Cloud Composer DAG for log export: Vertex AI Model Monitoring automatically collects prediction logs from the endpoint when request-response logging is enabled; a separate DAG is not required.
- Custom container image: Vertex AI Model Monitoring is a fully managed service; users configure it via the API or Console, not by providing a custom container image.

questions.question:
The operations team maintains a 500 GB log dataset in Cloud Storage that must be parsed, filtered by event type, and joined with a small reference table before being written to BigQuery for model training. The preprocessing logic is straightforward SQL-expressible transformations. The team has no Apache Spark infrastructure and wants to minimise operational overhead.

Which preprocessing tool is MOST appropriate for this workload?

choices.text: A local pandas script that reads the 500 GB file in chunks, applies the filter, merges with the reference table in memory, and writes the output to Cloud Storage
choices.explanation: Pandas in-memory processing is unsuitable for 500 GB data; memory constraints would cause the job to fail or require prohibitive chunking complexity.

choices.text: A Dataflow pipeline written in Apache Beam that reads each log file from Cloud Storage, applies ParDo transforms for parsing and filtering, and writes to BigQuery
choices.explanation: Dataflow is appropriate for streaming or complex stateful pipelines; for straightforward SQL-expressible batch transformations at this scale, BigQuery SQL is simpler and lower overhead.

choices.text: BigQuery SQL with a CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE statement that loads the Cloud Storage files via a BigQuery external table, applies the filter and join, and writes the result to a native table
choices.explanation: BigQuery can query Cloud Storage files as external tables and execute SQL joins and filters at petabyte scale with no infrastructure to manage.

choices.text: A Dataproc cluster running Apache Spark that reads the Cloud Storage files, executes SparkSQL transformations, and writes the output to BigQuery
choices.explanation: Dataproc adds cluster management overhead and is more suited to workloads where Spark-native features are needed; BigQuery SQL covers this use case without infrastructure management.

questions.domain: Collaborating Within and Across Teams to Manage Data and Models
skills: 2.1.2: Choosing the right tool for data preprocessing based on scale and complexity (e.g., BigQuery [SQL], Dataflow, Apache Spark, and in-memory Python frameworks).
questions.tip: When transformations can be expressed in SQL and the data already lives near BigQuery, consider which tool eliminates the most infrastructure overhead.
questions.explanation:
BigQuery can treat Cloud Storage files as external tables and execute SQL filters, joins, and aggregations at scale without any cluster management. For SQL-expressible batch preprocessing at 500 GB, it is the lowest-overhead option.

**Why it works:** BigQuery's serverless architecture handles parallelism automatically; there is no cluster to provision or tune.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Pandas in-memory: 500 GB exceeds typical memory limits; chunking adds complexity without solving the scale problem.
- Dataflow: powerful for streaming and complex stateful transforms, but adds pipeline code complexity that SQL already handles here.
- Dataproc/Spark: adds cluster provisioning overhead for a workload that SQL can handle more simply.

questions.question:
The ML team needs to preprocess 500 GB of raw clickstream logs stored in Cloud Storage before training. Each log record requires stateful aggregation: computing a 30-minute rolling session window per user, then extracting features from each session. A team member proposes using pandas in a Colab notebook. The senior engineer instead proposes the following approach.

```python
import apache_beam as beam
from apache_beam.transforms import window

with beam.Pipeline(runner='DataflowRunner', options=options) as p:
    sessions = (
        p
        | 'ReadLogs' >> beam.io.ReadFromText('gs://bucket/logs/*.json')
        | 'ParseJSON' >> beam.Map(parse_log)
        | 'AssignTimestamps' >> beam.Map(assign_ts)
        | 'WindowIntoSessions' >> beam.WindowInto(
              window.Sessions(gap_size=1800))
        | 'GroupByUser' >> beam.GroupByKey()
        | 'ExtractFeatures' >> beam.Map(extract_features)
        | 'WriteFeatures' >> beam.io.WriteToText('gs://bucket/features/')
    )
```

Why is Dataflow with Apache Beam the MOST appropriate choice for this workload compared to pandas?

choices.text: The Sessions window transform in Apache Beam is a proprietary algorithm unavailable in pandas, making Beam the only Python library capable of computing session-based features.
choices.explanation: Session windowing is a concept, not a proprietary Beam algorithm. The key reason to use Dataflow is distributed scale and managed infrastructure, not exclusive access to an algorithm.

choices.text: Dataflow automatically converts the Beam pipeline into optimised SQL queries that BigQuery executes, making it faster than any Python-based approach for log preprocessing.
choices.explanation: Dataflow executes Beam pipelines on managed VMs, not by converting to SQL. It does not route jobs through BigQuery.

choices.text: Dataflow runs the pipeline on managed distributed workers, handling 500 GB of data with session windowing that pandas cannot express at scale without loading all data into memory.
choices.explanation: Apache Beam on Dataflow distributes processing across many workers and natively supports stateful streaming operations like session windows. Pandas loads data into a single machine's RAM, making it impractical for 500 GB with stateful aggregation.

choices.text: Dataflow pipelines written in Python automatically apply GPU acceleration to the GroupByKey and Map transforms, reducing preprocessing time compared to CPU-bound pandas operations.
choices.explanation: Dataflow does not automatically use GPUs for Beam transforms. Its advantage for this workload is horizontal scalability across many CPU workers, not GPU acceleration.

questions.domain: Collaborating Within and Across Teams to Manage Data and Models
skills: 2.1.2: Choosing the right tool for data preprocessing based on scale and complexity (e.g., BigQuery [SQL], Dataflow, Apache Spark, and in-memory Python frameworks).
questions.tip: Consider what happens to pandas when the dataset exceeds the memory of a single machine and requires stateful windowed aggregation.
questions.explanation:
500 GB of data with stateful 30-minute session windowing per user exceeds what a single pandas process can handle in memory. Dataflow with Apache Beam distributes the pipeline across managed workers, supports native session window semantics via `beam.WindowInto(Sessions(...))`, and scales horizontally without any infrastructure management.

**Why it works:** Beam's session window abstraction handles the grouping and gap detection logic across a distributed cluster.

**Why the others don't work:**
- SQL conversion: Dataflow executes Beam graphs on workers, not via SQL.
- Proprietary algorithm: session windowing is a general concept; Beam's advantage is scale.
- GPU acceleration: not relevant here; Beam's value is horizontal CPU scaling.

questions.question:
An ML team is rolling out a new version of a high-stakes credit scoring model. Their rollout policy requires that the new model receives 5% of traffic for 48 hours, then 25% for another 48 hours, and only reaches 100% after the preceding stages show no degradation in precision and latency. If a stage fails, the previous model must be fully restored within minutes.

Which sequence of Vertex AI endpoint operations implements this CANARY deployment strategy?

choices.text: Deploy the new model version to the endpoint alongside the existing model; update the traffic split to 5/95, then 25/75, then 100/0 after each stage passes; if a stage fails, set the split back to 0/100 for the new model.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: Delete the existing model deployment and replace it with the new model, then roll back by re-deploying the old model from the registry if issues arise.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: Create a new endpoint for each stage, progressively shifting all traffic from the old endpoint to the new one by updating DNS records.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: Deploy the new model to a separate endpoint and run shadow traffic by duplicating all production requests to it without affecting the primary model's responses.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

skills: 4.1.4: Implementing model rollout strategies (e.g., A/B testing and canary deployments) to compare model versions.
questions.tip: A canary deployment gradually increases traffic to a new version in stages, with a rollback path if metrics degrade.
questions.explanation:
Incrementally adjusting the traffic split on a single endpoint while keeping both models deployed is the canonical canary deployment pattern on Vertex AI.

**Why it works:** Both models remain deployed throughout the rollout, so reverting to 0/100 instantly restores full traffic to the existing model without any redeployment delay. Each staged split is a lightweight API call that takes effect in seconds.

**Why the others don't work:**
- New endpoint per stage with DNS: DNS TTLs introduce propagation delays that prevent the minutes-level rollback required; also does not leverage the native traffic split feature.
- Shadow traffic to a separate endpoint: Shadow mode validates the new model's outputs but does not expose it to real production traffic, so business metrics cannot be measured.
- Delete and redeploy: Removing the existing deployment means rollback requires a full redeployment cycle, which can take several minutes and violates the quick-restore requirement.

questions.question:
During a review of the company's AI strategy, the ML team is asked to select a foundation model from Model Garden for a customer-facing summarization service. The service will process 50,000 documents per day, each up to 10 pages long. Cost per token is a primary concern and the team wants to avoid fine-tuning.

Which TWO factors should the team evaluate first when comparing Gemini variants in Model Garden for this use case? (Select 2)

choices.text: Multimodal input support for images and audio within the selected Gemini variant.
choices.explanation: The source documents are text-only; multimodal capabilities provide no advantage for this workload.

choices.text: Availability of supervised fine-tuning support for each Gemini variant.
choices.explanation: The team explicitly ruled out fine-tuning, so this criterion is irrelevant to the selection decision.

choices.text: Per-token pricing for input and output tokens across available Gemini variants.
choices.explanation: At 50,000 documents per day, even small differences in per-token cost compound significantly; this is the primary cost lever.

choices.text: Number of model parameters to estimate quality relative to model size.
choices.explanation: Model Garden does not expose raw parameter counts as a selection criterion, and parameter count alone does not predict summarization quality or cost.

choices.text: Maximum context window size to confirm the model can process a full 10-page document in one API call.
choices.explanation: A context window too small for 10-page documents forces chunking, which increases complexity and may increase total token usage.

skills: 1.2.1: Evaluating and selecting the appropriate model for a given task from Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Model Garden.
questions.tip: High-volume batch workloads have different priorities than interactive workloads - focus on what drives cost and throughput at scale.
questions.explanation:
For a high-volume summarization workload, input token pricing and output token length are the two most direct cost drivers, and context window must be sufficient for 10-page documents.

**Why it works:** Evaluating per-token pricing between Gemini Flash and Gemini Pro directly impacts the cost of 50,000 daily documents. Confirming the context window can fit 10 pages (roughly 8,000-15,000 tokens) ensures the model can process each document in a single call without chunking.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Model parameter count: parameter count is not directly exposed in Model Garden selection and does not reliably predict cost or summarization quality.
- Availability of supervised fine-tuning: the team explicitly wants to avoid fine-tuning, making this criterion irrelevant.
- Multimodal input support: the documents are text-based; multimodal capability adds no value here.

questions.question:
A team trained a regression model using a TFX pipeline. The Transform component was used to normalize numeric features and compute vocabulary-based encodings during training. After deployment, the team notices that prediction requests processed by a separate custom preprocessing service produce different feature values than those used during training, leading to degraded model performance.

What is the ROOT CAUSE of this training-serving skew?

choices.text: The serving model is loaded from a different Cloud Storage path than the training model artifact
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: The serving infrastructure is not using the SavedModel preprocessing graph exported by the TFX Transform component
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: The ExampleValidator component did not flag schema anomalies in the serving data
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: The Evaluator component thresholds were set too loosely, allowing a poorly calibrated model to be promoted
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

skills: 5.1.3: Ensuring consistent data preprocessing between training and serving.
questions.tip: The TFX Transform component exports two artifacts after processing: a transformed dataset for training and a reusable preprocessing graph for serving.
questions.explanation:
The root cause is that the serving infrastructure is using a custom preprocessing service instead of the SavedModel preprocessing graph that TFX Transform exported during training.

**Why it works:** TFX Transform produces a SavedModel that encapsulates the exact same normalization and encoding logic applied during training. When this graph is loaded at serving time (for example, by attaching it to the model or by calling it in a Vertex AI custom prediction routine), the feature values are guaranteed to be computed identically. Using any separate preprocessing implementation risks subtle differences in logic, vocabulary ordering, or numeric precision.

**Why the others don't work:**
- The Evaluator component thresholds were set too loosely: Evaluator gates model promotion on quality metrics; it does not affect feature preprocessing at serving time.
- The ExampleValidator component did not flag schema anomalies: ExampleValidator detects data anomalies before training; it does not prevent preprocessing inconsistencies at serving time.
- The serving model is loaded from a different Cloud Storage path: Using a different model artifact would cause incorrect weights, not a preprocessing mismatch. The question specifically describes feature value differences consistent with preprocessing skew.

questions.question: Match each Vertex AI Feature Store resource to its primary role in the feature creation and serving workflow.

choices.text: Selects a subset of Features from one or more Feature Groups and materialises them into an online store on a defined sync schedule
choices.explanation: A Feature View defines which features are served and controls the sync from BigQuery to the online store.

choices.text: Wraps a BigQuery table or view as the source of truth for a set of related feature attributes

choices.text: Schedules and monitors the execution of data preprocessing pipelines that produce feature values

choices.text: Provides the low-latency infrastructure used to serve feature values at inference time
choices.explanation: A Feature Online Store is the serving backend that stores materialised feature values for fast lookup during prediction.

choices.text: Represents a single named attribute within a Feature Group, corresponding to one column in the source table
choices.explanation: A Feature is the atomic unit of metadata in Feature Store, describing one measurable attribute of an entity.

skills: 2.1.3: Creating and consolidating features in Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Feature Store.

Vertex AI Feature Store has a clear hierarchy: Feature Groups reference BigQuery sources, Features name individual attributes, Feature Views select and sync subsets into an online store, and the Feature Online Store provides the low-latency serving layer.

questions.question:
An e-commerce platform wants to build a product recommendation system. User interaction logs contain 200 million events across 50 million users and 2 million products. The team requires low-latency online recommendations and needs the model to capture complex, non-linear user-item interactions. Training budget is generous, but inference must complete in under 50 ms.

Which model type BEST satisfies the latency and interaction-complexity requirements?

choices.text: LLM with retrieval-augmented generation
choices.explanation: LLM inference latency is typically hundreds of milliseconds to seconds per query, which exceeds the 50 ms budget without aggressive caching and approximations.

choices.text: Logistic regression with hand-crafted features
choices.explanation: Logistic regression cannot capture the non-linear, high-dimensional interaction patterns at 50 M users x 2 M items scale without impractical feature engineering.

choices.text: ARIMA
choices.explanation: ARIMA is a univariate time-series model and cannot model user-item interactions or produce ranked recommendation lists.

choices.text: DNN-based two-tower retrieval model
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

skills: 3.1.1: Choosing the model type (e.g., ARIMA, DNN, and LLM).
questions.tip: Consider which architecture can learn high-dimensional embedding spaces from implicit feedback at scale while still producing fast inference through approximate nearest-neighbor lookup.
questions.explanation:
A DNN-based two-tower model learns separate embedding towers for users and items, enabling sub-millisecond approximate nearest-neighbor retrieval at serving time, making it the standard architecture for large-scale recommendation.

**Why it works:** The two-tower architecture decouples user and item representations, so item embeddings are pre-computed offline and served via an ANN index. Query latency is dominated only by the user tower forward pass plus ANN lookup, easily fitting within 50 ms.

**Why the others don't work:**
- ARIMA: Designed for univariate sequential time-series, not multi-entity collaborative filtering.
- LLM with RAG: Generative inference latency far exceeds the 50 ms requirement at the scale described.
- Logistic regression: Cannot learn non-linear feature interactions at this dimensionality without extensive, brittle manual feature engineering.

questions.question:
The operations team at a logistics company needs to forecast daily parcel volumes at 150 regional depots for the next 30 days. Four years of daily volume data is stored in BigQuery by depot and date. The team wants to minimise infrastructure overhead and keep predictions queryable via SQL.

Which BigQuery ML model type is MOST suitable for this workload?

choices.text: ARIMA_PLUS with the time_series_id_col option set to the depot identifier, producing per-depot forecasts in a single training job.
choices.explanation: ARIMA_PLUS supports multi-series forecasting via time_series_id_col, auto-tunes seasonality and trend, and outputs forecasts queryable with ML.FORECAST.

choices.text: BOOSTED_TREE_REGRESSOR trained on manually engineered lag features for each depot to predict the next 30 daily values.
choices.explanation: Boosted trees can model regression but require manual lag feature engineering and do not natively produce multi-horizon forecasts, adding significant complexity.

choices.text: LINEAR_REG with one-hot encoded depot IDs and date components such as day-of-week and month.
choices.explanation: Linear regression cannot capture autocorrelation or complex seasonality without extensive manual feature engineering, producing lower-quality forecasts than ARIMA_PLUS for time-series data.

choices.text: KMEANS to cluster depots by volume patterns and assign future volumes based on cluster centroids.
choices.explanation: k-means is an unsupervised clustering algorithm and does not produce time-series forecasts. It cannot predict future values.

skills: 1.1.1: Building models in BigQuery ML or Agent Platform AutoML (e.g., classification, regression, forecasting, and clustering) based on the business problem.
questions.tip: Think about which BigQuery ML model type is purpose-built for multi-series time-based prediction.
questions.explanation:
ARIMA_PLUS is BigQuery ML's native time-series model. The time_series_id_col option allows a single model to produce separate forecasts for each depot without training one model per series.

**Why it works:** ARIMA_PLUS automatically handles trend, seasonality, and holiday effects. ML.FORECAST returns predicted values per series queryable via standard SQL.

**Why the others don't work:**
- BOOSTED_TREE_REGRESSOR: can regress on tabular features but requires manual lag engineering and outputs only single-step predictions.
- LINEAR_REG: lacks autocorrelation modelling; underfits seasonal patterns without heavy feature engineering.
- KMEANS: unsupervised clustering — it does not forecast numeric outcomes.

questions.question:
During a review of the company's AI strategy, the ML team is asked to select a foundation model from Model Garden for a customer-facing summarization service. The service will process 50,000 documents per day, each up to 10 pages long. Cost per token is a primary concern and the team wants to avoid fine-tuning.

Which TWO factors should the team evaluate first when comparing Gemini variants in Model Garden for this use case? (Select 2)

choices.text: Availability of supervised fine-tuning support for each Gemini variant.
choices.explanation: The team explicitly ruled out fine-tuning, so this criterion is irrelevant to the selection decision.

choices.text: Per-token pricing for input and output tokens across available Gemini variants.
choices.explanation: At 50,000 documents per day, even small differences in per-token cost compound significantly; this is the primary cost lever.

choices.text: Number of model parameters to estimate quality relative to model size.
choices.explanation: Model Garden does not expose raw parameter counts as a selection criterion, and parameter count alone does not predict summarization quality or cost.

choices.text: Maximum context window size to confirm the model can process a full 10-page document in one API call.
choices.explanation: A context window too small for 10-page documents forces chunking, which increases complexity and may increase total token usage.

choices.text: Multimodal input support for images and audio within the selected Gemini variant.
choices.explanation: The source documents are text-only; multimodal capabilities provide no advantage for this workload.

skills: 1.2.1: Evaluating and selecting the appropriate model for a given task from Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Model Garden.
questions.tip: High-volume batch workloads have different priorities than interactive workloads - focus on what drives cost and throughput at scale.
questions.explanation:
For a high-volume summarization workload, input token pricing and output token length are the two most direct cost drivers, and context window must be sufficient for 10-page documents.

**Why it works:** Evaluating per-token pricing between Gemini Flash and Gemini Pro directly impacts the cost of 50,000 daily documents. Confirming the context window can fit 10 pages (roughly 8,000-15,000 tokens) ensures the model can process each document in a single call without chunking.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Model parameter count: parameter count is not directly exposed in Model Garden selection and does not reliably predict cost or summarization quality.
- Availability of supervised fine-tuning: the team explicitly wants to avoid fine-tuning, making this criterion irrelevant.
- Multimodal input support: the documents are text-based; multimodal capability adds no value here.

questions.question:
An ML team is rolling out a new version of a high-stakes credit scoring model. Their rollout policy requires that the new model receives 5% of traffic for 48 hours, then 25% for another 48 hours, and only reaches 100% after the preceding stages show no degradation in precision and latency. If a stage fails, the previous model must be fully restored within minutes.

Which sequence of Vertex AI endpoint operations implements this CANARY deployment strategy?

choices.text: Deploy the new model version to the endpoint alongside the existing model; update the traffic split to 5/95, then 25/75, then 100/0 after each stage passes; if a stage fails, set the split back to 0/100 for the new model.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: Create a new endpoint for each stage, progressively shifting all traffic from the old endpoint to the new one by updating DNS records.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: Deploy the new model to a separate endpoint and run shadow traffic by duplicating all production requests to it without affecting the primary model's responses.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

choices.text: Delete the existing model deployment and replace it with the new model, then roll back by re-deploying the old model from the registry if issues arise.
choices.explanation: See question-level explanation for details.

skills: 4.1.4: Implementing model rollout strategies (e.g., A/B testing and canary deployments) to compare model versions.
questions.tip: A canary deployment gradually increases traffic to a new version in stages, with a rollback path if metrics degrade.
questions.explanation:
Incrementally adjusting the traffic split on a single endpoint while keeping both models deployed is the canonical canary deployment pattern on Vertex AI.

**Why it works:** Both models remain deployed throughout the rollout, so reverting to 0/100 instantly restores full traffic to the existing model without any redeployment delay. Each staged split is a lightweight API call that takes effect in seconds.

**Why the others don't work:**
- New endpoint per stage with DNS: DNS TTLs introduce propagation delays that prevent the minutes-level rollback required; also does not leverage the native traffic split feature.
- Shadow traffic to a separate endpoint: Shadow mode validates the new model's outputs but does not expose it to real production traffic, so business metrics cannot be measured.
